Bell-clapper loss of contact

Words: 83
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
Let a bell have axial moment of inertia Mk2 and centre of mass h from its axle. A clapper of point mass m at radius l touches the bell at fixed relative angle β. While they remain in contact, the clapper angle θ from the upward vertical obeys (Mk2+ml2)θ¨=Mghsin(θ−β)+mglsinθ. The contact force opposing increasing angle is N=mgsinθ−mlθ¨. Eliminating the acceleration gives
N=Mk2+ml2mMg​[k2sinθ−lhsin(θ−β)].
(1)
The first zero on the physical trajectory marks detachment, because a nonadhesive contact cannot support negative normal force. Selecting the correct trigonometric branch is part of the contact problem.

Major-axis relaxation theorem (T≥L2/(2Imax​))

Words: 58
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
At fixed angular momentum, rotational energy is minimized by rotation about the largest principal moment of inertia. Indeed, T=∑i​Li2​/(2Ii​)≥∑i​Li2​/(2Imax​). Weak internal dissipation can therefore relax a nearly rigid isolated body towards that axis. A perfectly rigid torque-free body conserves energy and does not settle; both extreme-inertia axes are stable in its ideal dynamics. The maximum-inertia axis need not be the geometrically longest axis.

Centre of percussion (b=IO​/(Mh))

Words: 141 Articles: 1
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
For a body constrained to rotate about a fixed pivot, a perpendicular impulse K delivered at distance b from the pivot produces ω=Kb/IO​. If the centre of mass is distance h from the pivot, its momentum is Mωh. The pivot impulse is JO​=Mωh−K, and vanishes when b=IO​/(Mh). This impact location is the centre of percussion. The result assumes the stated planar rigid-body geometry and a short impulse; it is not a claim that all forces at the pivot vanish afterward.

Hinge impulse of an edge-pivoted square plate (JH​=K(3a/(2l)−1/4))

Words: 64
Centre of percussion OurBigBook.com
For a uniform square plate of side l hinged along an edge, h=l/2 and IH​=Ml2/3. An impulse K normal to the plate, applied a distance a below the centre, gives vG​=3K(1+2a/l)/(4M) and signed hinge impulse JH​=K(3a/(2l)−1/4). Therefore the hinge impulse vanishes at a=l/6 below the centre, a distance 2l/3 from the hinge. The sign of JH​ identifies the reaction direction; its magnitude is ∣JH​∣.

Words: 38
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
A rigid body with moment of inertia I, constant driving power P and linear resisting torque −γω has an exponential approach of ω2 to P/γ. The ideal drive requires torque P/ω, so starting from rest is a limiting energy model with singular initial torque.

Vehicle rollover threshold (vmax​=gaRb​/h​)

Words: 60
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
For a rigid vehicle turning on a level road, with centre of mass height h, half track width a and turn radius Rb​, sufficient static friction supplies centripetal acceleration v2/Rb​. The inner and outer wheel normal forces obey Ni​+No​=Mg and a(No​−Ni​)=Mhv2/Rb​. The inner contact force first vanishes at the displayed speed. The approximation neglects suspension movement and extra torques; inadequate static friction can cause sliding before rollover.

Two hinged rods with both ends sliding on a floor (vhinge​=6glsinα​)

Words: 92
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
Two identical uniform rigid bodies of rod shape, each of length 2l and mass M, form a symmetric arch with a free common hinge and both outer ends sliding without friction on a horizontal floor. At angle θ, each center has speed l∣θ˙∣, giving total kinetic energy 4Ml2θ˙2/3. The total gravitational potential energy is 2Mglsinθ. Conservation of energy from rest at α gives the displayed hinge impact speed. Unlike fixing one outer endpoint, allowing both endpoints to slide keeps the arch center horizontally fixed. The floor reaction on each rod is Mg[1+9sin2θ−6sinαsinθ]/4, nonnegative throughout this fall.

Endpoint collision of two freely rotating equal rods (J=2mV(1+e)​,∣ω∣=4ℓV(1+e)​)

Words: 75
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
Each massless rod has endpoint masses m at distance ℓ from its centre, hence total mass 2m and moment of inertia 2mℓ2. In a symmetric opposite-end collision with centres approaching at speed V, a horizontal impulse J changes each centre speed by J/(2m) and each contact-point speed by J/m. The coefficient of restitution gives 2J/m−2V=2eV. Both rods rotate in the same sense for the staggered vertical configuration; their centre speeds after impact are V(3−e)/4.

Two hinged rods sliding on a floor (θ˙2=2l3g​1+3sin2θsinα−sinθ​)

Words: 86
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
Two equal uniform rods of length 2l and mass M, one pivoted to the floor and the other endpoint sliding on it, have arch coordinates B=(2lcosθ,2lsinθ) and C=(4lcosθ,0). The kinetic energy decomposition about the center of mass gives T=34​Ml2(1+3sin2θ)θ˙2, while gravitational potential energy is 2Mglsinθ. Conservation of energy from rest at angle α gives the displayed equation and hinge impact speed 6glsinα​, provided contact is maintained. The endpoint's normal reaction becomes negative during this constrained fall if sinα>35/54; a unilateral floor then permits detachment and the constrained formula no longer describes the entire motion.

Solid-body rotation (Ω=constant)

Words: 28
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
In solid-body rotation the angular velocity is independent of distance from the rotation axis, so tangential speed is proportional to cylindrical radius. A galactic region with this galaxy rotation curve has radial epicyclic frequency κ=2Ω.

Symmetric top

Words: 355 Articles: 9
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
A symmetric top is a rigid body with two equal principal moments of inertia, conventionally I1​=I2​. Its third principal axis is its symmetry axis.

Prolate symmetric top

Words: 18
Symmetric top OurBigBook.com
A rotor with two equal transverse moments and a smaller symmetry-axis moment, Ia​<Ib​=Ic​. Its rotational constants obey A>B=C.

Oblate symmetric top (I1​=I2​<I3​)

Words: 31
Symmetric top OurBigBook.com
An oblate symmetric top has two equal smaller principal moments of inertia and a larger moment of inertia about its symmetry axis. A planar trigonal molecule, such as boron trifluoride, is an example. Its axial rotational constant is smaller than its transverse rotational constant.

Torque-free precession of a symmetric top (ϕ˙​=L/I⊥​)

Words: 117 Articles: 1
Symmetric top OurBigBook.com
For an axially symmetric rigid body with I1​=I2​=I⊥​ and I3​=I∥​, no external torque means that angular momentum L is fixed in an inertial frame. The axial angular velocity ω3​ is constant by Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body, and the symmetry axis obeys
e˙3​=I⊥​L​×e3​.
(2)
Its angle to L is constant and it precesses in space at L/I⊥​. The transverse angular-velocity components instead rotate in body coordinates at signed rate (I∥​−I⊥​)ω3​/I⊥​. These are different frame descriptions and must not be substituted for one another.

Body-frame and space-frame frequencies of free symmetric-top precession

Words: 39
Torque-free precession of a symmetric top OurBigBook.com
For principal inertias I⊥​,I⊥​,I∥​, the transverse angular-velocity components rotate in body axes at signed rate (I∥​−I⊥​)ω3​/I⊥​. The symmetry axis precesses about the inertially fixed angular momentum at rate L/I⊥​. These are different frame-dependent descriptions of the same motion.

A heavy symmetric top is a symmetric top with one point fixed in a uniform gravitational field. Its vertical and body-axis rotational symmetries give two cyclic Euler angles.

Heavy symmetric top OurBigBook.com
Writing the unit symmetry axis as n and axial spin momentum as s=I3​ω3​, angular momentum is L=I1​n×n˙+sn. Taking its derivative and applying gravitational torque gives I1​n×n¨+sn˙=−mgℓn×z.

Nutation (θ(t))

Words: 40
Heavy symmetric top OurBigBook.com
Variation in the inclination of a rotating body's axis, distinguished from its azimuthal precession. For a heavy symmetric top, the cyclic angular momenta reduce the motion to μ˙​2=F(μ) with μ=cosθ and F cubic. Its admissible interval and turning points describe the nutation.

Uniform precession of a heavy symmetric top (I1​cosθΩ2−I3​ω3​Ω+Mgl=0)

Words: 69 Articles: 1
Heavy symmetric top OurBigBook.com
A heavy symmetric top precesses uniformly when its inclination is constant and its azimuthal speed is constant. For a nonvertical inclination, the condition is I1​cosθΩ2−I3​ω3​Ω+Mgl=0. The real-root condition depends on whether the body axis points above or below the horizontal.

The time for a precessing orientation to turn through 2π. An unlabelled line is unchanged by a π turn, so its visible pattern can repeat after half the full precession period.

Angular velocity is the vector whose direction gives the instantaneous rotation axis and whose magnitude gives the angular speed.

Angular acceleration (α=dω/dt)

Words: 36
Angular velocity OurBigBook.com
Angular acceleration is the time derivative of angular velocity, α=dω/dt. For rotation about a fixed axis, its signed scalar component obeys τ=Iα when the axial moment of inertia is constant and τ is the total applied torque about that axis.

Angular speed (ω=∣ω∣)

Words: 35
Angular velocity OurBigBook.com
Angular speed is the nonnegative magnitude of angular velocity: ω=∣ω∣. It measures the rate of rotation about an instantaneous axis without specifying its direction. For uniform circular motion of radius R, the ordinary speed is v=Rω.

A fixed space frame is an inertial orthonormal basis whose axes do not rotate with the body.

Principal body frame

Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
A principal body frame is an orthonormal basis fixed in the body and aligned with the principal axes of its inertia tensor. In this frame the inertia tensor is diagonal with principal moments I1​,I2​,I3​.

Principal axis

Words: 18
Principal body frame OurBigBook.com
A principal axis is an eigenvector direction of the inertia tensor. Choosing three orthogonal principal axes diagonalizes the inertia tensor.

ω˙32​=−I1​I2​I32​[L2−2EI2​+I3​(I2​−I3​)ω32​][L2−2EI1​+I3​(I1​−I3​)ω32​]​.

Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body OurBigBook.com
For principal moments I1​=I2​=I and symmetry-axis unit vector e3​, angular momentum and angular velocity obey

Intermediate axis theorem

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body OurBigBook.com
For a rigid body with three distinct positive principal moments of inertia 0<I1​<I2​<I3​ and zero external torque about its centre of mass, steady rotation about the first or third principal axis is Lyapunov stable in angular velocity, while rotation about the intermediate principal axis is unstable. Here steady rotation means ω=Ωe^i​ in the principal body frame, with constant Ω=0. A small sideways perturbation remains small about the extreme principal moments of inertia, but generically grows about the intermediate one. Stable does not mean that the wobble decays: without damping, there is no asymptotic stability. Coincident principal moments of inertia and a stationary body are excluded.[ref]
No external torque is needed for a body to tumble. Conservation of angular momentum fixes L in the fixed space frame, but the body can turn relative to L, so its angular velocity components in the principal body frame change. The torque-free rigid-body invariants constrain this motion. A supported gyroscope with gravitational torque has different governing assumptions.
Fixed-angular-momentum energy test for principal-axis rotation (ΔT=21​J12​(I1−1​−I3−1​)+21​J22​(I2−1​−I3−1​))
Words: 79
Intermediate axis theorem OurBigBook.com
For torque-free rotation, total angular momentum magnitude J and rotational kinetic energy are conserved. Near rotation about principal axis three, eliminate J32​=J2−J12​−J22​ from T=∑i​Ji2​/(2Ii​) to obtain the displayed energy difference from J2/(2I3​). If I3​ is largest, it is a constrained energy minimum; if smallest, a maximum. Both extrema are stable in the conservative problem. An intermediate moment gives opposite signs in the quadratic form, a saddle and instability. Dissipation changes the fixed-energy argument and must not be silently added to torque-free motion.
Normalized intermediate-axis model ((I1​,I2​,I3​)=(1,2,3))
Words: 188
Intermediate axis theorem OurBigBook.com
Choose an inertia unit I∗​ and an angular speed unit Ω∗​>0, so physical principal moments of inertia are I∗​(1,2,3), physical angular velocity is Ω∗​ω, and normalized time is t=Ω∗​tphysical​. The Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body become
ω˙1​=−ω2​ω3​,ω˙2​=ω3​ω1​,ω˙3​=−31​ω1​ω2​.
(9)
This is a physically admissible ideal planar mass distribution: I3​=I1​+I2​ is the perpendicular axis theorem. A book of finite thickness need not have these exact ratios.
For an original comparison, start with angular velocity (1,ε,0), (ε,1,0) or (ε,0,1), respectively. With ε=0.01, the transverse Euclidean norm stays small about axes one and three, but becomes order one about axis two. For the intermediate-axis start, its linearization gives
ω1​≃εcosh(t/3​),ω3​≃−3​ε​sinh(t/3​),ω2​≃1.
(10)
The hyperbolic functions contain a growing exponential function with rate λ2​=1/3​. Reducing ε tenfold delays reaching the same small transverse amplitude by approximately 3​log10≃3.99 normalized time units, once the growing term dominates. That delays the instability. Once the transverse angular velocity is comparable to the main component, the linearization ceases to describe the motion.
Torque-free tumbling (c2​=e^2​⋅L^)
Words: 294
Intermediate axis theorem OurBigBook.com
A useful readout of a tumble is the alignment of the intermediate principal axis e^2​ with the conserved angular momentum direction L^. In the principal body frame, write Li​=Ii​ωi​ and L=∣L∣. Then
c2​(t)=e^2​(t)⋅L^=LL2​(t)​.
(11)
A change from c2​≃+1 to c2​≃−1 means that the directed body axis has turned nearly 180∘ relative to L. It does not mean that L reversed in the fixed space frame. The unsigned line through that principal axis hides this distinction, so a marked end matters in an actual demonstration.
For the normalized intermediate-axis model with ω(0)=(0.01,1,0), the rotational kinetic energy and squared angular momentum are E=1.00005 and L2=4.0001. Hence L2−2EI2​=−0.0001: this initial condition lies close to, but off, the intermediate-axis separatrix. An independent calculation evolves L˙body​=Lbody​×I−1Lbody​ and a rotation matrix taking body components to space components. The intermediate principal axis crosses c2​=0 at normalized times approximately 10.3773 and 31.1319, alternating long nearly aligned intervals with quicker reversals.
Both calculations use step size 0.005 without rescaling either invariant. Over 0≤t≤50, the tumbling calculation changes rotational kinetic energy and squared angular momentum by less than 4×10−13 relative to their initial values. Reconstructing L in the fixed space frame gives relative error below 3×10−12. Halving the step changes the body components and rotation matrix entries by less than 3×10−10. These checks distinguish physical tumbling from numerical drift. On the exact intermediate-axis separatrix, approach to an intermediate-axis rotation takes infinite time; the recurrent off-separatrix example here is different.
Spinning-book demonstration
Words: 217
Intermediate axis theorem OurBigBook.com
Clemson's documented apparatus is a book held tightly closed with several rubber bands. Toss it freely with spin about each principal axis in turn: the stated visual readout is steady orientation for the smallest and largest principal moments of inertia, but a flip before the catch for the intermediate one. The same book and the two extreme-axis throws provide comparison controls; the bands support the rigid body approximation by restraining the pages. This is a documented qualitative demonstration, not a measurement of λ2​.[ref]
For a rectangular book with length a, width b and thickness c, where a>b>c, a uniform mass model gives principal moments of inertia M(b2+c2)/12, M(a2+c2)/12 and M(a2+b2)/12. The intermediate principal axis runs across the width through the centre of mass; the maximum is normal to the cover. A marked cover or end helps distinguish ordinary spin from reversal of a directed body axis.
Interpret only the interval after release and before the catch: hand contact applies torque, whereas gravity in a uniform gravitational field has zero net torque about the centre of mass because ∫rdm=0. Air resistance, page motion, an imperfect release and short flight limit the approximation. A toss ending before the perturbation grows need not reveal instability. Comparable initial angular speeds and flight durations would improve the comparison; these are suggested controls, not quantified controls reported by Clemson.
Linear stability of principal-axis rotation
Words: 230
Intermediate axis theorem OurBigBook.com
For 0<I1​<I2​<I3​, the transverse linear stability rates about steady rotation with signed component Ω=0 are
ν1​=∣Ω∣I2​I3​(I2​−I1​)(I3​−I1​)​​,ν3​=∣Ω∣I1​I2​(I3​−I2​)(I3​−I1​)​​,λ2​=∣Ω∣I1​I3​(I2​−I1​)(I3​−I2​)​​.
(12)
Axes one and three have transverse eigenvalues ±iν1​ and ±iν3​, producing bounded oscillations. Axis two has transverse eigenvalues ±λ2​, giving growing and decaying exponential functions. A neutral longitudinal perturbation corresponds to a small change of Ω. Generic intermediate-axis disturbances contain a growing component; a precisely chosen decaying direction is exceptional. For the normalized intermediate-axis model with ∣Ω∣=1, the values are ν1​=1/3​, ν3​=1 and λ2​=1/3​.
Proof outline: the linearization of the Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body about the third principal axis gives transverse perturbations obeying
ω˙1​=I1​I2​−I3​​Ωω2​,ω˙2​=I2​I3​−I1​​Ωω1​,
(13)
and hence
ω¨1​=−Ω2I1​I2​(I3​−I2​)(I3​−I1​)​ω1​.
(14)
Cyclic permutation gives the other rates. For nonlinear Lyapunov stability of the extreme rotations, use the torque-free rigid-body invariants: the conserved quadratic forms L2−2I1​E and 2I3​E−L2 have strictly positive transverse coefficients about axes one and three respectively. They bound transverse angular velocity, while E bounds its longitudinal change near nonzero rotation. Imaginary transverse eigenvalues alone would not establish this nonlinear conclusion.[ref]
The practical lesson is to choose a stable principal axis when using rotation to maintain an instrument's pointing direction. Both extreme principal moments of inertia are stable in the ideal torque-free model; if internal damping lowers rotational kinetic energy while approximately preserving angular momentum, the minimum energy E=L2/(2I3​) instead favors the largest principal moment of inertia. A control system must account for torque, changing mass distributions and flexibility before applying this ideal result.
Intermediate-axis separatrix
Words: 36

The moment of inertia about a specified axis measures how a mass distribution resists changes of angular velocity about that axis. For point masses mi​ at perpendicular distances r⊥i​, or a continuous distribution with mass density ρ,

Its SI unit is kgm2. The distance is to the entire axis, not to one point on it: moving a point mass along the axis leaves its contribution unchanged. The moment of inertia depends on both the distribution and the chosen axis; it is not determined by total mass alone. About an axis fixed in an inertial frame, a rigid body with larger moment of inertia has smaller angular acceleration under the same net axial torque, and greater rotational kinetic energy at the same angular speed.[ref]
For a simple model, put four equal point masses of total mass M on light rigid spokes at radius a. Their moment of inertia is Ma2. Doubling a quadruples the moment of inertia without changing M. The illustrated placements a=R/3 and a=R give MR2/9 and MR2. Actual spokes and finite-sized weights contribute their own moments of inertia; the point mass model neglects them. Repositioning weights during rotation also breaks the fixed-distribution assumption, so it requires a separate work and angular momentum calculation.
The moment of inertia of a uniform disc follows by dividing it into concentric annuli: dm=(2M/R2)rdr and I=∫0R​r2(2M/R2)rdr=MR2/2. For an ideal thin ring every mass element is at R, so I=MR2. A ring of finite radial thickness instead uses the moment of inertia of a uniform annulus, I=M(R2+b2)/2, with inner radius b. A moment of inertia is thus a compact summary of radial placement rather than a complete description of shape. For several joined pieces, their moments of inertia add only when each is calculated about the same axis.[ref]
A physical pendulum makes the moment of inertia measurable through timing. Martín Monteiro, Cecilia Stari, Cecilia Cabeza and Arturo C. Martí used a metal bar with suspension holes 1.0cm apart and an attached smartphone. They report bar length 1.199m, bar mass 0.2518kg and phone mass 0.1311kg. Changing the suspension hole changes the pivot axis. Their readouts were phone gyroscope angular velocity records, analyzed by autocorrelation or a fit to a sinusoid, and an independent photogate; the logged records for the sinusoid fits lasted 10s. They observed agreement between the three timing methods and the geometry-based model, including a minimum of oscillation period as the suspension point varied. These are reported apparatus details and observations, not measurements made for this article.[ref]
To infer a moment of inertia from such a measurement, determine the total mass Mtot​ including every attached part, locate the assembly's centre of mass G, and measure its distance h>0 below the horizontal pivot O. Record successive crossings in the same direction, or the elapsed time tN​ for N complete oscillations, giving oscillation period P=tN​/N. The physical pendulum model with a fixed pivot, a uniform gravitational field, negligible friction and the small-angle approximation gives

The parallel axis theorem converts the inferred pivot moment of inertia to one about a parallel axis through G. The controls and interpretation of that comparison are described there. If one principal moment of inertia vanishes in an ideal line-mass model, this constant-energy surface is unbounded in that direction and is no longer an ellipsoid.
The rotational energy ellipsoid gives the geometry behind Poinsot's ellipsoid, but a constant-energy surface alone does not determine a free-rotation trajectory. A torque-free trajectory must also satisfy the conserved angular momentum constraint and the Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body.

Words: 159

If two principal moments of inertia coincide, for example I1​=I2​=I3​, every direction in their two-dimensional eigenspace is a principal axis. The perpendicular axis is determined, but there is no privileged orthogonal pair within that plane. Rotating the pair in the plane leaves the diagonal inertia tensor unchanged. If all three principal moments of inertia coincide, IO​=I0​1 and every axis through O is principal. This follows from the eigenvalue multiplicity and eigenspace, rather than from a failure of diagonalization. [ref]
Equal principal moments of inertia do not prove that a body's outline has continuous rotational symmetry. For example, six equal point masses at (±a,0,0), (0,±a,0) and (0,0,±a) have IO​=4ma21. This discrete layout has the same axial moment of inertia in every direction, although its actual mass distribution changes under most rotations. Conversely, even when all three principal moments of inertia are distinct, principal axes are unoriented lines: reversing an eigenvector's sign gives the same axis. Near repeated eigenvalues, small measurement errors can rotate fitted principal axes substantially within the nearly degenerate eigenspace, so quoted directions need an uncertainty assessment as well as quoted principal moments of inertia.

The parallel axis theorem transfers a moment of inertia from an axis through the centre of mass G to a parallel axis through O:

The axis for IG​ must pass through the centre of mass; IO​ may refer to an axis outside the body. No uniform-density or planar-shape assumption is needed. Within any family of parallel axes, the centre of mass axis minimizes the moment of inertia.[ref]
A short proof isolates why the centre of mass matters. Choose parallel axes perpendicular to an xy plane, put G at the origin, and place O at (d,0). Then
IO​=∫[(x−d)2+y2]dm=IG​−2d∫xdm+d2∫dm=IG​+Md2,
(35)
because ∫xdm=0 in centre of mass coordinates. Individual mass elements can move closer to the new axis, but their weighted cross terms cancel. For arbitrary parallel axes A and B, use IB​−IA​=M(dB2​−dA2​), where each distance is measured from the parallel centre of mass axis; adding M times the squared separation of A and B is generally incorrect. A displacement along the axis has d=0. Changing the axis direction instead requires the inertia tensor or, in its applicable planar setting, the perpendicular axis theorem.
For a uniform disc, mass M and radius R, the central perpendicular moment of inertia is IG​=MR2/2. Shifting that axis to the rim gives d=R and IO​=3MR2/2, three times IG​. In the computed M=2kg, R=0.30m example, IG​=0.090kgm2, Md2=0.180kgm2 and IO​=0.270kgm2. At angular speed 10rad/s the rim-pivoted disc has rotational kinetic energy 13.5J. Its centre of mass now moves, so 21​IO​ω2 already includes that translation; adding a separate centre of mass translation term to it would count that contribution twice.
The physical pendulum measurement described under moment of inertia provides a practical check: infer IO​=Mgh(P/2π)2 at several pivot positions, then subtract Mh2 to obtain IG​. Keep all pivot axes parallel and measure h to the centre of mass of the entire moving assembly. The same assembly should yield the same IG​ within measurement precision. If a smartphone is attached, its mass and its own moment of inertia belong in both the geometric prediction and the centre of mass calculation. The published bar-and-phone study explicitly adds both contributions using the parallel axis theorem.[ref]
For a careful replication, release small swings without a push, repeat timings at several small amplitudes, and check that the extrapolated oscillation period is stable as amplitude decreases. Time many complete oscillations and repeat the run; two crossings of a photogate per cycle must not be mistaken for two cycles. Inspect decay of amplitude and compare early and late timings to detect significant pivot friction or air drag. Mark the bar and phone mount to detect relative slip, tighten the attachment, and check that the pivot support does not rock or migrate between holes. Repeat with an independent photogate or video readout to check the phone's timing. These are proposed controls for the replication, not additional results reported by the authors. The ideal model excludes appreciable damping, large swings and flexing; subtraction of Mh2 also magnifies relative errors when IG​ is much smaller than IO​.
The oscillation period need not increase monotonically with pivot distance: the shift raises the moment of inertia but also increases the gravitational restoring torque. For a computed slender uniform bar model of length L, IG​=ML2/12 and
4π2P2​=g1​(h+12hL2​),h>0.
(36)
This expression has its minimum at h=L/12​. With L=1m, h=0.50m and stipulated g=9.81m/s2, the prediction is P≃1.638s; it is not a recorded timing or a prediction for the bar with a phone attached. The competing terms explain why a timing experiment can reveal a mass distribution rather than merely its weight.

Lagrange, Euler, and Kovalevskaya tops

Words: 51
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
The Lagrange, Euler, and Kovalevskaya tops are three integrable cases of fixed-point rigid body dynamics. The Euler top has no external torque; the Lagrange top has axial symmetry and its center of mass on the symmetry axis; the Kovalevskaya top has two equal principal moments twice the third and its center of mass in the corresponding principal plane.

Euler angles ((ϕ,θ,ψ))

Words: 233 Articles: 7
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
Euler angles describe the orientation of a rigid body through three successive angular rotations. Their convention specifies the axes and order of the rotations. For a symmetric top, a common convention takes θ as the inclination, ϕ as precession and ψ as spin about the body axis.

Euler angles for a symmetric top

Words: 190 Articles: 6
Euler angles OurBigBook.com
With the convention in which θ is inclination, ϕ is precession, and ψ is body-axis spin, an axisymmetric body's kinetic energy is
T=2I​(θ˙2+sin2θϕ˙​2)+2J​(ψ˙​+cosθϕ˙​)2.
(42)

Heavy symmetric top Lagrangian

Words: 164 Articles: 5
Euler angles for a symmetric top OurBigBook.com
For a fixed point a distance a from the centre of mass and inclination measured from the upward vertical,
L=T−Mgacosθ.
(43)
The spin and precession angles are cyclic.
This is the Lagrangian of a Lagrange top, one of the Lagrange, Euler, and Kovalevskaya tops.
Lagrange top
Words: 62 Articles: 1
Heavy symmetric top Lagrangian OurBigBook.com
A Lagrange top is an axisymmetric rigid body with one point fixed on its symmetry axis, moving in a uniform gravitational field with its center of mass on that axis.

Lagrange top OurBigBook.com
For a Lagrange top whose inclination θ is measured from the upward vertical, steady precession at angular speed Ω obeys
I1​Ω2cosθ−pψ​Ω+Mgl=0.
(44)
Thus steady precession at a prescribed 0<θ<π/2 exists precisely when
pψ2​≥4MglI1​cosθ.
(45)

With transverse and axial moments I,J, the Hamiltonian is
H=2Ipθ2​​+2Isin2θ(pϕ​−pψ​cosθ)2​+2Jpψ2​​+Mgacosθ.
(46)

Words: 51 Articles: 1

Fixing the cyclic momenta pψ​=λ and pϕ​=μ leaves the canonical pair (θ,pθ​) and a one-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian with effective potential
Vλ,μ​(θ)=2Isin2θ(μ−λcosθ)2​+2Jλ2​+Mgacosθ.
(47)

Heavy symmetric top reduction OurBigBook.com
At the upright spinning state, pϕ​=pψ​=λ. The reduced potential is locally minimized at zero inclination when
λ2>4IMga,

so sufficiently large axial angular momentum stabilizes the gravitationally inverted top.

Rolling without slipping

Words: 954 Articles: 15
Rigid body dynamics OurBigBook.com
Rolling without slipping imposes that the contact point is instantaneously at rest, giving v=R omega.

Rolling-cylinder loop contact threshold (hmin​=11(R−a)/4)

Words: 145 Articles: 1
Rolling without slipping OurBigBook.com
A solid cylinder rolling inside a circular loop has centre-path radius ℓ=R−a, kinetic energy 3mv2/4, and speed v2=4g[h−ℓ(1−cosθ)]/3 at angle θ from the bottom. The normal contact force is smallest at the top. Requiring vt2​≥gℓ gives the displayed necessary contact threshold under imposed no-slip rolling. The centre's maximum acceleration on the circle is at the bottom, and at the threshold it is 11g/3 upward. This is a limiting contact condition, not a guarantee for arbitrary finite static friction or an unspecified approach curvature.

Finite-friction qualification of a marginal rolling loop

Words: 67
Rolling-cylinder loop contact threshold OurBigBook.com
At the limiting release height for a solid cylinder, the loop normal force is N=(7mg/3)(1+cosθ) and the required static-friction magnitude is mg∣sinθ∣/3. Thus ∣f∣/N=∣sinθ∣/[7(1+cosθ)] diverges near the top, even though both forces vanish there. A finite friction coefficient therefore requires a height above the ideal contact threshold to maintain no-slip rolling throughout. A question imposing rolling but giving no coefficient determines the ideal limiting bound, not a realistic friction-dependent minimum.

Rolling constraint inside a moving circular track (rψ˙​=Rθ˙−(R−r)ϕ˙​)

Rolling without slipping OurBigBook.com
A circular body of radius r rolls inside a circular track of radius R. Let θ be the track's material rotation, ϕ the absolute angle of the line joining the two centres, and ψ the inner body's absolute spin angle, all with one consistent orientation. Equating contact-point velocities gives the displayed constraint. Translation of the track's centre cancels from that equality. A stationary track gives ψ˙​=−(R−r)ϕ˙​/r.

The final rolling speed is uf​=5J(1+d/a)/(7M), independent of a positive constant friction coefficient; friction can accelerate an initially overspinning centre of mass.

A ball bearing transfers loads through rolling spherical elements between two races. The no-slip conditions at both contacts determine the translation and spin of each ball; these are generally not the same angular velocity.

Rolling ball between concentric races (vcm​=Rω/2)

Words: 53
Ball bearing OurBigBook.com
If an inner race of radius R rotates at angular velocity ω and an outer race is stationary, a ball of radius r rolling at both contacts has centre speed Rω/2 and spin −Rω/(2r). Its centre follows a circle of radius R+r. The angular momentum about the common race axis includes both orbital angular momentum and spin.

T=21​Mv2+21​Iω2=21​(M+r2I​)v2.

Pulley coupled to a rolling disc (q=g(m−Msinθ)/(m+3M/2))

Words: 78
Effective mass of a rolling rigid body OurBigBook.com
A hanging mass m pulls the centre of a uniform disc of mass M up an incline of angle θ, using a light string and light frictionless pulley. If the disc rolls without slipping and the string is parallel to the slope, its effective translational mass is M+I/a2=3M/2. With downward hanging acceleration q, q=g(m−Msinθ)/(m+3M/2). Static friction has signed downslope component Mq/2 and supplies the rolling torque. The acceleration threshold is unchanged from a sliding block, although rotational inertia reduces the magnitude.

Spring-mounted rolling cylinder ((m+I/R2)x¨+bx˙+kx=0)

Words: 96
Rolling without slipping OurBigBook.com
Attach a spring of spring constant k to the axle of a round body of mass m, radius R and axial moment of inertia I. Assume rolling without slipping, a horizontal drag force −bx˙ applied through the axle, and no additional resisting torque. The translational force equation is mx¨=−kx−bx˙+f, where f is signed static friction. The rotational equation and rolling constraint give f=−Ix¨/R2, yielding the displayed equation. Equivalently, the kinetic energy is (m+I/R2)x˙2/2. This added effective inertia lowers the undamped angular frequency to k/(m+I/R2)​. A distributed viscous torque would add a separate damping term and cannot be inferred from the drag force alone.

Rolling-time factor on a straight incline (troll​/tslide​=1+I/(MR2)​)

Rolling without slipping OurBigBook.com
For a rigid body rolling from rest down a straight incline with fixed rolling radius R and axial moment of inertia I, translation and rotation give (M+I/R2)s¨=Mgsinθ. A smooth slide has s¨=gsinθ. Travel over the same distance from rest therefore gives the displayed time ratio. Static friction must suffice for rolling without slipping; its contact point is at rest, so this ideal friction does no work. A uniform solid cylinder has I=MR2/2 and ratio 3/2​.

For rolling without slipping, its speed is b∣θ˙∣. Combining translation and rotation gives kinetic energy 21​(IG​+mb2)θ˙2. Slipping solid cylinder on an incline (tanα>3μ)

Words: 74
Rolling without slipping OurBigBook.com
For a uniform solid cylinder, take s positive uphill and ω positive for uphill rolling without slipping. The velocity of the contact point is w=s˙−aω. Uphill kinetic friction gives s¨=−g(sinα−μcosα) and aω˙=−2μgcosα. Starting from s˙(0)=aω(0), one obtains w=−gt(sinα−3μcosα). Thus tanα>3μ makes the assumed uphill kinetic friction self-consistent for the entire ascent and descent. Without slip the required uphill static friction is mgsinα/3; it is available exactly when tanα≤3μ under the same limiting coefficient.

A round body of radius R0​ in a fixed cylinder of radius R1​ has center of mass path radius a=R1​−R0​. With orbital angle θ and spin angular velocity Ω both positive about the same axis, rolling without slipping gives aθ˙+R0​Ω=0. For moment of inertia I=γmR02​, its kinetic energy is 21​ma2(1+γ)θ˙2. Release from rest at angle α gives, by conservation of energy, a descent time 1+γ​ times that of frictionless sliding along the same center of mass path. The spin sign reverses if its positive direction is chosen opposite to the orbital angle.

For rolling without slipping inside a stationary circular cylinder, take the inner body's axial moment of inertia to be I=γmr2. Its center of mass follows a circle of radius d=R−r, and the reduced Lagrangian is L=m(1+γ)d2θ˙2/2−mgd(1−cosθ). The Euler-Lagrange equation gives (1+γ)dθ¨+gsinθ=0. Linearizing near the lowest position yields the displayed small oscillation frequency. A uniform solid cylinder has γ=1/2. This reduction requires sustained contact and enough static friction to prevent slipping.
